questions.prompt: A node holds labels [0, 0, 1, 1]. What are its Gini impurity and entropy (in bits)?
questions.explanation: Gini = 1 − (0.5² + 0.5²) = 0.5. Entropy = −2·0.5·log2(0.5) = 1 bit. Both are at their maximum for two classes.

questions.prompt: Why weight each child's impurity by n_child / n when computing information gain?
options: So that a split peeling off a single pure row doesn't look artificially good
To make entropy and Gini give identical results
questions.explanation: Without weights, a one-row pure child counts as much as the large mixed child, which rewards splits that separate almost nothing.

questions.prompt: You draw a bootstrap sample of n rows from a dataset of n rows. Roughly what fraction of the distinct original rows does it contain for large n?
questions.explanation: Each row is missed with probability (1 − 1/n)ⁿ ≈ 1/e ≈ 0.368, so about 63.2% appear at least once. The rest are out-of-bag.

questions.prompt: What does a random forest add on top of plain bagging of trees?
options: Random feature subsets at each split, which decorrelate the trees
Weighting trees by their training accuracy
questions.explanation: Restricting each split to a random subset of features keeps strong features from dominating every tree, so the votes are less correlated and average out better.
